--- unit: "C" chapter: "09" lecture: "09c" metadata-files: - ../../_slide-settings.yml format: revealjs: theme: default --- ::: {.my-title} # [Statistical Methods]{.blue} Polynomial Regression ::: {.my-grey} [Unit {{< meta unit >}} | Chapter {{< meta chapter >}}]{}
[Lecture {{< meta lecture >}}]{} ::: ::: {.my-attrib} {{< meta attribution >}} ::: ![](../../img/growth_curve_357EDD.png){.absolute bottom=30 right=0 width="400"} ::: ::: {.cell} ::: # Overview ## Motivation {.fs90} - So far, we have always fit [straight lines]{.b} between $y$ and $x$ variables - But sometimes the correct functional form is [curved]{.b .red} in some way - If we fit a straight line anyway, our results may be very biased ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](c_Slides_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-1-1.png){width=864} ::: ::: ## Linear regression ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} fit <- lm(y2 ~ x, data = df2) # data from right panel of slide 3 model_parameters(fit) ## Parameter | Coefficient | SE | 95% CI | t(98) | p ## ------------------------------------------------------------------- ## (Intercept) | -4.54 | 0.43 | [-5.39, -3.70] | -10.66 | < .001 ## x | 1.19 | 0.14 | [ 0.90, 1.47] | 8.29 | < .001 r2(fit) ## # R2 for Linear Regression ## R2: 0.412 ## adj. R2: 0.406 ``` ::: ## Visualizing the model ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} library(modelbased) plot(estimate_relation(fit, by = "x"), show_data = TRUE) ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](c_Slides_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-4-1.png){width=960} ::: ::: ## Assumption checking ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} check_model(fit, check = "linearity") ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](c_Slides_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-6-1.png){width=960} ::: ::: ## Conclusions {.fs90} - Linear regression did not work well for predicting $y_2$ - The functional form diagnostic looked bad for the latter - The $R^2$ for the latter was worse than we could do ::: {.fragment} - We need to change our functional form! - We need to allow a curve in our function - This is what polynomial regression does ::: # Polynomial Regression ## Power polynomials {.fs70} - LM can handle simple curves through **power polynomial** transformations! - We will add predictors that are *power transformations* of other predictors $$\hat{y} = b_0 + b_1 \color{red}{x^1} + b_2 \color{red}{x^2} + \cdots + b_d \color{red}{x^d}$$ - Each term has a **degree** equal to its exponent + e.g., $x^1$ is the *first* degree term and $x^2$ is the *second* degree term + Note that $x^1=x$ and $x^0=1$, which can be thought of as the intercept + The term with the highest exponent is the **highest degree term** + All other terms are referred to as the **lower degree terms** ## Number of bends {.fs90} - The highest degree term determines the curve's overall shape + The number of bends is equal to $(d-1)$ ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](c_Slides_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-7-1.png){width=960} ::: ::: ## Direction of curvature {.fs90} - The sign $(\pm)$ of the curve's highest degree term's slope
determines its **direction of curvature** (i.e., up or down) ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](c_Slides_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-8-1.png){width=960} ::: ::: # Quadratic Regression ## Expanding the equation {.fs90} - A quadratic relationship requires two predictors to represent $x$ $$\hat{y} = b_0 + b_1 x^1 + b_2 x^2$$ - The **highest** degree coefficient determines the overall shape + $b_2$: Does the curve bend up $(+)$, down $(-)$, or not at all $(0)$? ::: {.pv2} - The **lower** degree coefficients fine-tune the position and shape + $b_1$: What is the slope of the curve's tangent line at $x=0$? + $b_0$: What is the intercept of the curve's tangent line at $x=0$? ::: ## Quadratic regression 1 - We use the `I()` function to do math inside the formula ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} fit1b <- lm(y1 ~ x + I(x^2), data = df1) model_parameters(fit1b) ## Parameter | Coefficient | SE | 95% CI | t(97) | p ## ----------------------------------------------------------------- ## (Intercept) | 0.27 | 0.15 | [-0.02, 0.57] | 1.82 | 0.072 ## x | 1.13 | 0.04 | [ 1.05, 1.20] | 30.43 | < .001 ## x^2 | 3.05e-03 | 0.01 | [-0.03, 0.03] | 0.21 | 0.838 r2(fit1b) ## # R2 for Linear Regression ## R2: 0.908 ## adj. R2: 0.906 ``` ::: ::: {.fs90} The $x^2$ slope is NOT significant, so the curve is NOT needed ::: ## Visualizing the model ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} plot(estimate_relation(fit1b, by = "x"), show_data = TRUE) ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](c_Slides_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-11-1.png){width=960} ::: ::: ## Assumption checking ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} check_model(fit1b, check = "linearity") ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](c_Slides_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-13-1.png){width=960} ::: ::: ## Quadratic regression 2 ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} fit2b <- lm(y2 ~ x + I(x^2), data = df2) model_parameters(fit2b) ## Parameter | Coefficient | SE | 95% CI | t(97) | p ## ------------------------------------------------------------------- ## (Intercept) | -0.16 | 0.31 | [-0.77, 0.45] | -0.53 | 0.599 ## x | 1.27 | 0.07 | [ 1.13, 1.40] | 18.85 | < .001 ## x^2 | -0.50 | 0.03 | [-0.55, -0.44] | -18.71 | < .001 r2(fit2b) ## # R2 for Linear Regression ## R2: 0.872 ## adj. R2: 0.870 ``` ::: - The $x^2$ slope is significant, so the curve is needed! - Because the slope is negative, it will bend downward ## Visualizing the model ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} plot(estimate_relation(fit2b, by = "x"), show_data = TRUE) ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](c_Slides_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-16-1.png){width=960} ::: ::: ## Assumption checking ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} check_model(fit2b, check = "linearity") ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](c_Slides_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-18-1.png){width=960} ::: ::: ## Visualizing the tangent line ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](c_Slides_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-19-1.png){width=960} ::: ::: ## Calculating extrema - It may be useful to know the maximum or minimum values ::: {.columns} ::: {.column} What value of $x$ gives the
most extreme value of $y$? $$x_m = \frac{-b_1}{2b_2}$$ ::: ::: {.column} What is the most extreme value of $y$ in the function? $$\hat{y}_m = \frac{4 b_2 b_0 - b_1^2}{4 b_2}$$ ::: ::: ## Calculating extrema {.fs90} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} model_parameters(fit2b) ## Parameter | Coefficient | SE | 95% CI | t(97) | p ## ------------------------------------------------------------------- ## (Intercept) | -0.16 | 0.31 | [-0.77, 0.45] | -0.53 | 0.599 ## x | 1.27 | 0.07 | [ 1.13, 1.40] | 18.85 | < .001 ## x^2 | -0.50 | 0.03 | [-0.55, -0.44] | -18.71 | < .001 b_0 <- -0.16 b_1 <- 1.27 b_2 <- -0.50 x_m <- (-b_1) / (2 * b_2) x_m ## [1] 1.27 yhat_m <- ((4 * b_2 * b_0) - b_1^2) / (4 * b_2) yhat_m ## [1] 0.64645 ``` ::: ## Visualizing extrema ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](c_Slides_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-21-1.png){width=960} ::: ::: # Adding Predictors ## Adding another predictor {.fs90} ::: {.cell replace_path='["../../data/",""]'} ```{.r .cell-code} library(tidyverse) screentime <- read_csv("../../data/screentime.csv") fit3 <- lm( mental_wellbeing ~ play_wd + I(play_wd^2) + deprived_area, data = screentime ) model_parameters(fit3) ## Parameter | Coefficient | SE | 95% CI | t(2996) | p ## ---------------------------------------------------------------------------- ## (Intercept) | 46.57 | 0.27 | [46.05, 47.09] | 175.27 | < .001 ## play wd | 2.22 | 0.29 | [ 1.65, 2.80] | 7.58 | < .001 ## play wd^2 | -0.34 | 0.05 | [-0.44, -0.23] | -6.18 | < .001 ## deprived area [yes] | -0.55 | 0.35 | [-1.24, 0.15] | -1.55 | 0.122 ``` ::: - The effects of `play_wd` are significant controlling for `deprived_area` - The effect of `deprived_area` is *not* significant controlling for `play_wd` and its square ## Visualizing the model {.fs90} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} plot(estimate_relation(fit3, by = c("play_wd", "deprived_area")), show_data = TRUE) ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](c_Slides_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-24-1.png){width=960} ::: ::: ## Adding moderation {.fs90} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} fit4 <- lm( mental_wellbeing ~ play_wd + I(play_wd^2) + deprived_area + play_wd:deprived_area + I(play_wd^2):deprived_area, data = screentime ) model_parameters(fit4) ## Parameter | Coefficient | SE | 95% CI | t(2994) | p ## ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- ## (Intercept) | 46.74 | 0.29 | [46.17, 47.31] | 160.84 | < .001 ## play wd | 2.06 | 0.40 | [ 1.27, 2.85] | 5.13 | < .001 ## play wd^2 | -0.34 | 0.08 | [-0.50, -0.19] | -4.36 | < .001 ## deprived area [yes] | -0.98 | 0.46 | [-1.87, -0.09] | -2.15 | 0.032 ## play wd × deprived area [yes] | 0.47 | 0.59 | [-0.69, 1.63] | 0.80 | 0.427 ## play wd^2 × deprived area [yes] | -0.01 | 0.11 | [-0.23, 0.20] | -0.13 | 0.896 ``` ::: - The effects of `play_wd` are not moderated by `deprived_area` ## Visualizing the model ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} plot(estimate_relation(fit4, by = c("play_wd", "deprived_area"))) ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](c_Slides_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-27-1.png){width=960} ::: ::: # Closing Thoughts ## Consider the range - You may only see *part* of the curve in your sample! ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](c_Slides_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-28-1.png){width=768} ::: ::: ## Advice {.fs90} - Models with higher degrees are more flexible + But they may overfit (fail to generalize) + They will be harder to interpret and justify - **Theory** should be used to decide between shapes + Quadratics can model processes with best/worst regions + Cubics can model opponent processes and regulation - Centering your $x$ variable is very helpful here + Also see `poly()` for orthogonal polynomials - Don't omit the lower degree terms/coefficients

<script>
  // htmlwidgets need to know to resize themselves when slides are shown/hidden.
  // Fire the "slideenter" event (handled by htmlwidgets.js) when the current
  // slide changes (different for each slide format).
  (function () {
    // dispatch for htmlwidgets
    function fireSlideEnter() {
      const event = window.document.createEvent("Event");
      event.initEvent("slideenter", true, true);
      window.document.dispatchEvent(event);
    }

    function fireSlideChanged(previousSlide, currentSlide) {
      fireSlideEnter();

      // dispatch for shiny
      if (window.jQuery) {
        if (previousSlide) {
          window.jQuery(previousSlide).trigger("hidden");
        }
        if (currentSlide) {
          window.jQuery(currentSlide).trigger("shown");
        }
      }
    }

    // hookup for slidy
    if (window.w3c_slidy) {
      window.w3c_slidy.add_observer(function (slide_num) {
        // slide_num starts at position 1
        fireSlideChanged(null, w3c_slidy.slides[slide_num - 1]);
      });
    }

  })();
</script>
